question: Do promotions significantly increase sales?
H0: For the same store x product, median daily units on promo days = on non-promo days
H1: Median daily units are higher on promo days (one-sided)
test: Wilcoxon signed-rank, paired by store x product (+ per category, Bonferroni)
why: Pairing compares a product with itself, so the mix of which products get promoted cannot fake a lift; daily unit counts are skewed, so a rank test is safer than a t-test.
effect: median lift +29%; rank-biserial r = 0.94; 93% of pairs gain
interpretation: Promotions raise units sold, and the effect is large (median +29%). Significant in 7/7 categories after Bonferroni: Snacks, Beverages, Household, Frozen, Personal Care, Groceries, Dairy. Strongest: Snacks (+65%).
action: Every planned promotion must increase that week's order by the category lift; promotion days are a required forecasting feature.

question: Does mean demand differ across store types?
H0: Daily demand per product has the same distribution in Express, Supermarket and Hypermarket stores
H1: At least one store type differs
test: Kruskal-Wallis + pairwise Mann-Whitney (Bonferroni); robustness: Friedman (product as block), ANOVA on log demand
why: Three groups and skewed demand -> rank test. Restricted to the 48 products sold in ALL formats, so differences in assortment cannot create a false difference.
effect: epsilon^2 = 0.42; median units/day: Express 5.7, Hypermarket 36.6, Supermarket 10.4
interpretation: Store format matters a lot: a Hypermarket sells 6.4x an Express store's volume of the same product. Pairwise (Bonferroni): Express vs Hypermarket p=1.44e-19; Express vs Supermarket p=8.24e-09; Hypermarket vs Supermarket p=7.92e-19. Friedman p = 1.43e-21, ANOVA(log) p = 2.21e-41 - same conclusion.
action: Reorder levels and safety stock must be set per store (format), never copied across stores; store_type is a required model feature.

question: Is stock-out frequency associated with promotion status?
H0: Stock-out status is independent of promotion status
H1: Stock-out status depends on promotion status
test: Chi-square test of independence (2x2) + odds ratio, Cramer's V; Mantel-Haenszel by store x category
why: Both variables are binary. With ~70k rows any tiny difference is 'significant', so the odds ratio is what we interpret. Mantel-Haenszel checks that it is not just because promoted products are in stock-out-prone stores/categories.
effect: stock-out rate 13.6% (promo) vs 5.2%; OR = 2.90; Cramer's V = 0.119; MH-adjusted OR = 3.01
interpretation: Promotion days have 2.9x the odds of a stock-out (3.0x after adjusting for store and category, MH p = 5.75e-216). Cramer's V is small because stock-outs are rare overall, but the business effect is large: stores are not ordering for promotions.
action: Link the promotions calendar to replenishment: raise stock before a promotion starts; promo_days_next_7 is a key stock-out feature.

question: Does temperature drive beverage demand?
H0: No monotonic association between daily temperature and beverage demand (rho = 0)
test: Spearman rank correlation, within each store (Bonferroni over 6 stores)
why: The relation need not be linear; testing within a store removes store-size differences.
effect: rho ranges 0.32 to 0.53; significant in 6/6 stores
interpretation: Hotter days sell more beverages in every store (strongest S01, rho = 0.53). p-value shown is the largest (weakest) of the six stores. Temperature also moves with season, so part of this is the summer effect.
action: Use the temperature forecast for beverage and frozen orders in summer.

question: Is late delivery associated with the supplier?
H0: Late delivery rate is the same for all 10 suppliers
H1: Late delivery rate differs by supplier
test: Chi-square test of independence (10 x 2) + odds ratio for the worst supplier vs the rest
why: Categorical supplier vs binary late/on-time outcome.
effect: SUP04 late 36% vs 7% others; OR = 7.7; Cramer's V = 0.32
interpretation: SUP04 is the outlier: 7.7x the odds of a late delivery. This explains why its category stocks out most.
action: Use SUP04's effective lead time (nominal + average delay) in reorder calculations and raise it with the supplier.

question: Do products that ran out in May keep running out after the June reorder recalibration?
H0: Jun-Aug stock-out rate is the same for combinations that stocked out in May and those that did not
H1: It is higher for combinations that stocked out in May (one-sided)
test: Mann-Whitney U on combination-level Jun-Aug stock-out rates
why: One value per store x product avoids treating 90 correlated days as independent; rates are skewed and many are 0.
effect: mean Jun-Aug stock-out rate 6.0% vs 2.6% (Mar-Apr: 9.0% vs 2.3%); rank-biserial r = 0.38
interpretation: Stock-outs are chronic: the combinations that ran out in May kept running out after the 1 June reset. The reset set levels from May sales, which were capped by empty shelves, so it under-corrected (see EDA chart 8 for the cover in days of sales vs days of estimated demand).
action: Recalibrate reorder levels on estimated demand (demand_est), and review every combination that stocked out in May.

question: Is weekend demand different from weekday demand?
H0: For the same store x product, median daily units on weekends = on weekdays
test: Wilcoxon signed-rank, paired by store x product, overall and per store format (Bonferroni)
effect: median weekend uplift: Express -6%, Hypermarket +45%, Supermarket +23%
interpretation: The weekend effect is real but its size depends on the format: Express p=2.76e-06; Hypermarket p=7.39e-14; Supermarket p=2.17e-34.
action: Deliveries should arrive before the weekend peak in the formats that have one; weekend days in the next 7 is a forecasting feature.
